title: Hypereia, the Phaeacians' first home
greek: ἐν εὐρυχόρῳ Ὑπερείῃ (en euruchorōi Hupereiēi)
short: The Phaeacians once lived in Hypereia ('Upland'), next to the Cyclopes, who plundered them until Nausithous led them away.
body: Hypereia is not otherwise located; its name may mean 'the land beyond' or 'the upper land', and it belongs to the same fabulous geography as the Cyclopes. The brief history matters for the poem's design. The Cyclopes, 'overweening' (huperēnoreontōn, a word Merry notes is normally used in the Odyssey of the suitors), represent strength without law, and the Phaeacians, harassed by them, emigrated to found an ordered city. Odysseus will tell the Phaeacians the story of his own encounter with the Cyclops Polyphemus in Book IX, an audience with good reason to appreciate it. Alcinous later claims kinship with both Cyclopes and Giants (7.205-6), and Polyphemus, like the Phaeacian royal line, is a son of Poseidon.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.4-5
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 6.4-6

title: Alphēstai: 'grain-earning men'
greek: ἑκὰς ἀνδρῶν ἀλφηστάων (hekas andrōn alphēstaōn)
short: Alphēstai, an old epithet of men, probably means 'earners' or 'grain-eaters'; Murray renders 'men that live by toil'.
body: The adjective is connected by most lexicographers with alphanein, 'to earn, bring in', and is often explained as 'gain-getting' or 'bread-eating', a description of ordinary mortals who must work the land for their food. The epithet sets the Phaeacians apart: they live 'far from' such men, in a land where the gods' gifts make the orchards bear all year (7.114-21) and where the people's work is sailing, weaving and pleasure. LSJ also records the ancient alternative derivation from alphi, 'barley-meal'. Either way the contrast is between toiling humanity and the near-divine ease of Scheria, the same contrast made explicitly in the description of Olympus a few lines later (6.41-7).

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 6.8

title: The founding of a colony
greek: ἀμφὶ δὲ τεῖχος ἔλασσε πόλει, καὶ ἐδείματο οἴκους, / καὶ νηοὺς ποίησε θεῶν, καὶ ἐδάσσατ᾽ ἀρούρας (amphi de teichos elasse polei ... kai edassat' arouras)
short: Nausithous' foundation of Scheria (wall, houses, temples, division of land) reads like a description of a Greek colonial foundation.
body: The lines list the acts of a founder (oikistēs) of the age of Greek colonisation, from the eighth century BC: leading out a people, walling the town, building houses and temples, and dividing the farmland into allotments. Merry explains edassato as 'allotted them for cultivation'. Irad Malkin and others have argued that the Phaeacian episode reflects the experience of colonial expansion in the west, at about the time the poem took shape; the Cyclopes' island in Book IX, fertile but uncultivated and without ships, is described from the same colonist's point of view (9.116-41). The name Nausithous, 'swift in ships', also fits a seafaring founder. This is the earliest Greek account of a city's foundation and is often cited by historians of colonisation.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.10
I. Malkin, The Returns of Odysseus: Colonization and Ethnicity (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1998)

title: Alcinous
greek: Ἀλκίνοος (Alkinoos)
short: Alcinous, king of the Phaeacians, has a name meaning 'strong of mind'; he becomes the model host of European literature.
body: The name combines alkē, 'strength', and noos, 'mind', and fits a king 'made wise in counsel by the gods' (6.12). Merry notes that, unlike most Phaeacian names, Alcinous, Arete and Laodamas are not drawn from seafaring. Alcinous is generous and dignified, sometimes a little pompous and over-ready to boast of his people, and his hospitality is the frame within which Odysseus tells his own adventures (Books IX-XII). His palace and gardens became proverbial: Milton compares the garden of Eden to the gardens of 'renowned Alcinous, host of old Laertes' son' (Paradise Lost 9.439-41), and the Phaeacians' ease was a byword for luxury in Horace (Epistles 1.2.28-31).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.111 (Phaeacian names)

title: Nausicaa
greek: Ναυσικάα (Nausikaa)
short: Nausicaa, Alcinous' daughter, has a ship-name like most Phaeacians; her meeting with Odysseus is one of the most admired episodes in Homer.
body: Like Nausithous, Nausicaa's name begins with naus, 'ship'. The second element is uncertain: it may come from kekasmai, 'to excel', giving something like 'excelling in ships', though other derivations have been proposed. She is unmarried, of marriageable age, and the poem allows a delicate undercurrent of romance: her dream is of washing clothes for a wedding (6.25-40), she wishes aloud that such a man might be her husband (6.244-5), and her father all but offers Odysseus her hand (7.311-15). The tension is resolved without loss of dignity in her farewell (8.457-68). Ancient readers imagined a sequel: some later writers reported a tradition that she married Telemachus. In modern literature she gave her name to Joyce's 'Nausicaa' episode in Ulysses and to Samuel Butler's theory of a female author of the Odyssey.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 6.17

anchor: gifted with beauty by the Graces
title: The Graces (Charites)
greek: Χαρίτων ἄπο κάλλος ἔχουσαι (Charitōn apo kallos echousai)
short: The Charites, Graces, are goddesses of beauty and charm; Nausicaa's two maids owe their beauty to them.
body: The Charites personify charis, the grace, charm and favour that make beauty attractive and gifts welcome. Homer has no fixed number or names for them: Merry observes that only one is named, Pasithea, promised to Sleep as a wife (Il. 14.267-9, 275-6); Hesiod later names three, Aglaea, Euphrosyne and Thalia (Theogony 907-9). They attend Aphrodite, who in Book VIII retires to Paphos where 'the Graces bathed her and anointed her' (8.364-6), and charis is the quality Athena sheds on Odysseus (6.235-7, 8.18-19). Two maids sleeping at the door are the conventional attendants of a well-born daughter; Penelope too never appears without two.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.18

title: The dream visitation
greek: στῆ δ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς (stē d' ar' huper kephalēs)
short: Athena enters Nausicaa's room 'like a breath of wind', stands over her head in a friend's likeness, and speaks to her in a dream.
body: This is a typical Homeric dream scene: the dream-figure 'stands over the head' of the sleeper, speaks, and departs, as with the Dream sent to Agamemnon (Il. 2.20-35), the ghost of Patroclus (Il. 23.68) and the phantom of Iphthime sent to Penelope (Od. 4.795-841). The simile 'like a breath of wind' can be set beside later images of swift, insubstantial movement such as Virgil's 'volucrique simillima somno' (Aeneid 2.794). Athena takes the form of the daughter of Dymas, a friend of Nausicaa's own age, and her message is adapted to its hearer: not 'go to the river and meet a stranger', but 'your wedding is near and your clothes are dirty'. This prospect of marriage is exactly the reason Nausicaa is too shy to name to her father (6.66-7).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.20, 6.22, 6.66
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 6.20-40

title: Washing clothes at the river
greek: πλυνοί (plunoi)
short: The princess herself takes the household's clothes to the washing-pits by the river: royal women in Homer do real domestic work.
body: The plunoi were tanks or trenches by a river through which clean water flowed; Merry describes them as dug beside the stream with a free flow in and out, and Homer mentions the stone washing-places of Troy at Iliad 22.153-6. The clothes were trampled in the water, spread to dry on the shingle, and the women bathed, oiled themselves and picnicked while they dried. That the king's daughter does this, driving the mule-cart herself, reflects the Homeric world in which aristocratic women spin, weave and manage the household's textiles: Arete is spinning at the hearth when Nausicaa goes to her father (6.52-3). Clothing is central to this episode: Odysseus arrives naked and receives clothes, and Arete will recognise the garments she made (7.233-9).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.86

anchor: Neither is it shaken by winds
title: Olympus, the untroubled home of the gods
greek: οὔτ᾽ ἀνέμοισι τινάσσεται οὔτε ποτ᾽ ὄμβρῳ / δεύεται (out' anemoisi tinassetai oute pot' ombrōi / deuetai)
short: Homer describes Olympus as a place beyond weather, always clear and bright, where the gods are happy all their days.
body: In the Iliad Olympus is a snowy mountain (Il. 1.420, 18.616). Here it is idealised into a celestial dwelling above wind, rain and snow, wrapped in cloudless brightness. Merry notes that the phrase 'where, they say' (hothi phasi) sounds strange from a poet who usually speaks of the gods with full authority, and discusses how the mountain-summit picture shades into a heavenly one. The passage was famous. Lucretius translated it for the abode of his Epicurean gods (De Rerum Natura 3.18-22), and Tennyson used it for the island-valley of Avilion in 'Morte d'Arthur' ('Where falls not hail, or rain, or any snow'). In context it contrasts sharply with the storm-tossed sea of Book V and the 'toiling men' just mentioned (6.8).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.42-6

title: 'Papa dear' (pappa phil')
greek: πάππα φίλ᾽ (pappa phil')
short: Nausicaa addresses her father with the child's word pappa, 'daddy', a rare touch of domestic intimacy in epic.
body: Pappa is a nursery word, like English 'papa'; the Iliad has only the verb pappazein, 'to say papa', of a warrior's children who will not greet their father on his return (Il. 5.408). Its use here gives the scene its charm. Nausicaa coaxes Alcinous with practical reasons (he needs clean clothes for the council, her brothers for dancing) while hiding her real thought of marriage, which Alcinous sees through and grants without comment (6.66-7). The exchange is one of the best-loved pieces of characterisation in Homer, and part of the Odyssey's general interest in household life, women and the young, which distinguishes it from the war-world of the Iliad.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.57

title: Nausicaa's modesty (aidōs)
greek: αἴδετο γὰρ θαλερὸν γάμον ἐξονομῆναι / πατρὶ φίλῳ (aideto gar thaleron gamon exonomēnai / patri philōi)
short: Aidōs, shame or modest respect, keeps Nausicaa from mentioning marriage; the same quality governs her whole conduct with the stranger.
body: Aidōs is a central Homeric value: the sense of what others will think, which restrains improper words and actions. Merry notes that the marriage Athena put into the dream is exactly the reason Nausicaa urges, and that it is aidōs that keeps her silent about it. The theme runs through the episode. Odysseus will not bathe before the maidens 'for I am ashamed' (6.221-2); Nausicaa will not be seen entering the city with a strange man because of gossip and reproach (6.273-88); and she says she would blame any girl who mixed with men 'before the day of open marriage'. Her conduct is a model of the propriety that makes the Phaeacian court a civilised contrast to the suitors' Ithaca.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.66

title: Ball-play and song
greek: σφαίρῃ ταὶ δ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ἔπαιζον ... τῇσι δὲ Ναυσικάα λευκώλενος ἤρχετο μολπῆς (sphairēi tai d' ar' epaizon ... tēisi de Nausikaa leukōlenos ērcheto molpēs)
short: The girls play a ball-game accompanied by song and dance, led by Nausicaa; a missed throw wakes Odysseus.
body: Molpē means song combined with rhythmic movement, and Merry sees no reason to doubt that the game was accompanied by a measured chant and dance. It is the earliest mention of ball-games in Greek literature, and the poem returns to the theme in Book VIII, where Alcinous' sons perform a dance with a purple ball (8.370-80). The game also has a plot function, managed by Athena: Nausicaa throws to a maid, misses, the ball falls into the river, the girls shriek, and Odysseus wakes (6.112-17). Nausicaa's epithet 'white-armed' (leukōlenos), used in the Iliad chiefly of Hera, marks the pale skin admired in women who live mostly indoors.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.100-1

title: Nausicaa like Artemis
greek: οἵη δ᾽ Ἄρτεμις εἶσι κατ᾽ οὔρεα ἰοχέαιρα, / ἢ κατὰ Τηΰγετον περιμήκετον ἢ Ἐρύμανθον (hoiē d' Artemis eisi kat' ourea iocheaira, / ē kata Tēügeton ... ē Erumanthon)
short: Nausicaa among her maids is compared to Artemis among her nymphs on the mountains, taller and lovelier than all; Virgil imitated it for Dido.
body: Artemis, the virgin huntress, ranges over Taygetus, the great range of Laconia, and Erymanthus in Arcadia, with the nymphs of the countryside, while her mother Leto rejoices. The comparison suits a maiden and prepares for Odysseus' own comparison of Nausicaa to Artemis (6.151-2). Virgil adapted it when Dido first appears among her people (Aeneid 1.498-502), as Merry notes. Ancient critics judged the imitation: Aulus Gellius reports, from pupils of the scholar Valerius Probus, the view that Virgil's version was less apt, since Homer's Nausicaa is at play in the countryside, while Dido is walking through her city on business, and Leto's joy has no point in Virgil (Attic Nights 9.9.12-17). The comparison of the two passages remains a classic exercise in how imitation changes meaning.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.102-9

title: The test of a people: hospitality and piety
greek: ἦ ῥ᾽ οἵ γ᾽ ὑβρισταί τε καὶ ἄγριοι οὐδὲ δίκαιοι, / ἦε φιλόξεινοι, καί σφιν νόος ἐστὶ θεουδής; (philoxeinoi, kai sphin noos esti theoudēs)
short: On every new shore Odysseus asks the same question: are the people violent and lawless, or hospitable and god-fearing?
body: These lines recur word for word when Odysseus lands on the Cyclops' island (9.175-6) and when he wakes on Ithaca (13.201-2), and Alcinous echoes them when he asks Odysseus to describe the peoples he has met (8.575-6). They define the axis on which the Odyssey judges societies: hubris and savagery versus xenia (the reciprocal bond between host and guest, protected by Zeus Xenios) and fear of the gods. The Phaeacians will pass the test (with some hesitation, 7.32-3), the Cyclops will fail it spectacularly, and the suitors in Ithaca will fail it in their own way. The adjective theoudēs, 'god-fearing', belongs to the moral vocabulary of the whole poem.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 6.119-21

title: Odysseus like a hungry lion
greek: βῆ δ᾽ ἴμεν ὥς τε λέων ὀρεσίτροφος (bē d' imen hōs te leōn oresitrophos)
short: Odysseus emerges from the bushes like a storm-beaten mountain lion driven by hunger; the girls scatter like sheep.
body: The lion simile belongs to the Iliad, where it describes warriors attacking; its lines closely resemble Sarpedon's assault on the Achaean wall (Il. 12.299-306). Transferred to a naked, salt-caked man approaching a group of girls, it is both alarming and slightly comic. Merry stresses the point of comparison: hunger drives Odysseus, as it drives the lion, to an unusual boldness. The simile shows how the girls see him, a wild thing from the woods, and it sets the problem he must solve: how to transform himself from a terrifying beast into a suppliant worth helping. Only Nausicaa stands firm, because Athena gives her courage. The leafy branch held for modesty (6.128-9) is a small sign of the civilised man under the wild exterior.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.130

title: Supplication: to clasp the knees or not
greek: ἢ γούνων λίσσοιτο λαβὼν εὐώπιδα κούρην (ē gounōn lissoito labōn euōpida kourēn)
short: Full supplication required clasping the knees; Odysseus decides that for a naked stranger to touch a young girl would offend, and pleads from a distance.
body: In the complete ritual the suppliant grasps the knees (and sometimes the chin) of the person he entreats, a gesture that makes refusal a breach of religious obligation. John Gould distinguished such 'complete' supplication from 'figurative' supplication with words alone. Odysseus' deliberation is a fine example of his social intelligence: the formal gesture would carry most force but could provoke anger in this situation. Merry records that the Alexandrian critic Athenocles suspected line 6.144, partly because of the repeated verb lissoito. Odysseus' speech, 'gentle and crafty' (meilichion kai kerdaleon, 6.148), is the poem's showpiece of persuasive flattery. He will perform the full ritual later, at Arete's knees (7.142).

sources.cite: J. Gould, 'Hiketeia', Journal of Hellenic Studies 93 (1973) 74-103
W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.144

title: 'Are you a goddess or a mortal?'
greek: γουνοῦμαί σε, ἄνασσα· θεός νύ τις ἦ βροτός ἐσσι; (gounoumai se, anassa; theos nu tis ē brotos essi?)
short: Odysseus opens with the supreme compliment: is she a goddess? If mortal, her family are thrice blessed. Virgil's Aeneas reuses the gambit.
body: The speech moves with great skill from flattery (comparison with Artemis) through blessing of her parents and her future husband, to a narrative of his own wonder at the palm at Delos, and only then to his plight and request (clothes, directions) and a closing blessing on her marriage. Virgil adapts the opening when Aeneas meets his disguised mother Venus in the woods near Carthage, 'o, quam te memorem, virgo? ... o dea certe' (Aeneid 1.327-9), with the irony that Venus really is a goddess. Odysseus himself says he 'fears greatly to touch thy knees', turning the abandoned gesture of supplication into a compliment.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.149
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 6.149-85

anchor: a young shoot of a palm
title: The palm at Delos
greek: Δήλῳ δή ποτε τοῖον Ἀπόλλωνος παρὰ βωμῷ / φοίνικος νέον ἔρνος (Dēlōi dē pote toion Apollōnos para bōmōi / phoinikos neon ernos)
short: Odysseus compares Nausicaa to a young palm he once saw beside Apollo's altar on Delos, the tree Leto clung to when she bore Apollo.
body: Delos was Apollo's birthplace: in the Homeric Hymn to Apollo, Leto gives birth clasping a palm tree (117-19), and a sacred palm was shown in the sanctuary for centuries afterwards. Merry notes that Cicero reported it still standing in his day (Laws 1.2). The comparison of a girl to a slender young plant (ernos) is traditional, but this one adds sacredness and wonder: Odysseus 'marvelled long' at the palm as he now marvels at her. His aside, 'on that journey on which evil woes were to be my portion', is a teasing glimpse of his identity, the first hint that this naked man led 'much people' to war. The palm image connects Nausicaa with Apollo's sister Artemis, to whom she has just been compared.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.162-7

title: Homophrosynē: like-mindedness in marriage
greek: ὁμοφροσύνην (homophrosunēn)
short: Odysseus wishes Nausicaa a husband, a home and homophrosynē, 'oneness of mind', the best thing in a marriage and a key value of the Odyssey.
body: The passage is the poem's fullest statement on marriage: nothing is better than when husband and wife 'keep house with one mind', a grief to their enemies and a joy to their friends, 'but they know it best themselves'. The ideal is enacted in the reunion of Odysseus and Penelope, who match each other in cunning and test each other's knowledge in the episode of the bed (23.173-230), and contrasted with the faithless Clytemnestra. Coming from a stranger to an unmarried girl, the wish is also a graceful farewell to any romantic possibility: it blesses her future marriage with someone else.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.181-2

title: Strangers and beggars come from Zeus
greek: πρὸς γὰρ Διός εἰσιν ἅπαντες / ξεῖνοί τε πτωχοί τε, δόσις δ᾽ ὀλίγη τε φίλη τε (pros gar Dios eisin hapantes / xeinoi te ptōchoi te, dosis d' oligē te philē te)
short: Nausicaa states the principle of xenia: every stranger and beggar is under the protection of Zeus, and even a small gift is welcome.
body: Merry explains pros Dios as 'sent by Zeus' or 'under the protection of Zeus'. Zeus in his aspect as Xenios protects strangers, and as Hikesios protects suppliants (cf. 7.164-5). The same couplet is spoken by the swineherd Eumaeus when he receives Odysseus disguised as a beggar (14.57-8), so the principle stated by a princess in Scheria returns in the humblest home in Ithaca, and the suitors' abuse of the beggar in their hall is measured against it. Nausicaa's reply as a whole (6.187-210) shows her good sense: she consoles him with the thought that Zeus allots fortune to good and bad alike, promises clothing and guidance, and rebukes her maids for running away.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.207
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 6.207-8

title: Hair like the hyacinth
greek: οὔλας ἧκε κόμας, ὑακινθίνῳ ἄνθει ὁμοίας (oulas hēke komas, huakinthinōi anthei homoias)
short: Athena makes Odysseus' hair fall in thick locks 'like the hyacinth flower'; whether the comparison is of colour or of curls is disputed.
body: The Homeric huakinthos is not certainly our hyacinth; it may be a kind of iris, larkspur or other dark-blue flower. Merry discusses both the identity of the flower and the point of comparison. Many interpreters take it as colour, dark hair like the dark petals, though Odysseus is called 'fair-haired' elsewhere (13.399, 431, where his locks will be withered as a beggar), which complicates that reading. Others think of the clustered, curling petals of the flower and hence of thick curls (oulas). The lines are repeated in Book XXIII (23.157-8), when Odysseus is beautified before Penelope, so the transformation that wins Nausicaa's admiration is also the prelude to the reunion with his wife.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.231

title: Gold laid over silver
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτε τις χρυσὸν περιχεύεται ἀργύρῳ ἀνήρ (hōs d' hote tis chruson pericheuetai arguroi anēr)
short: Athena sheds grace on Odysseus as a master craftsman, taught by Hephaestus and Athena, lays gold upon silver.
body: Merry explains the image as gold plated or inlaid on silver, a technique of luxury metalwork. The simile makes beauty a work of art and Athena an artisan; it pairs her with Hephaestus, the craftsman-god whose metalwork appears in Alcinous' palace (7.91-4) and in the song of Ares and Aphrodite (8.272-81). It is used again when Odysseus is beautified before Penelope (23.159-62). Virgil imitated the passage when Venus makes Aeneas beautiful before Dido: 'quale manus addunt ebori decus, aut ubi flavo / argentum Pariusve lapis circumdatur auro' (Aeneid 1.589-93). The transformation explains Nausicaa's change of view: 'Before he seemed to me uncouth, but now he is like the gods' (6.242-3).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.232

anchor: care not for bow or quiver
title: A people of ships, not bows
greek: οὐ γὰρ Φαιήκεσσι μέλει βιὸς οὐδὲ φαρέτρη, / ἀλλ᾽ ἱστοὶ καὶ ἐρετμὰ νεῶν (ou gar Phaiēkessi melei bios oude pharetrē, / all' histoi kai eretma neōn)
short: Nausicaa explains that her people have no interest in archery or war: their passion is ships, masts and oars.
body: The description of Scheria's harbours, assembly by the temple of Poseidon and ship-sheds (6.262-9) leads into this definition of the Phaeacians by what they lack. They are not warriors; in Book VIII Alcinous concedes that they are not even outstanding boxers or wrestlers, only runners, sailors and dancers (8.246-9). The bow is pointedly mentioned. Odysseus will boast of his archery to the Phaeacians (8.215-28), and the climax of the Odyssey is the contest of the bow in Book XXI and the slaughter of the suitors with it. The Phaeacians' pacifism is part of their idyllic, half-divine existence but also of their vulnerability (8.564-71).

anchor: Who is this that follows Nausicaa
title: The imagined gossip
greek: τίς δ᾽ ὅδε Ναυσικάᾳ ἕπεται καλός τε μέγας τε / ξεῖνος; (tis d' hode Nausikaai hepetai kalos te megas te / xeinos?)
short: Nausicaa imagines the malicious talk of a 'baser fellow' who sees her with the handsome stranger, and so asks Odysseus to follow at a distance.
body: Homeric characters often imagine what 'someone will say' (a so-called tis-speech), a device through which the poet expresses public opinion and the pressure of reputation. Irene de Jong has studied the device in the Iliad. Here it is used with great delicacy: the gossip voices exactly what Nausicaa herself half hopes, that the stranger is a husband she has found, or a god sent in answer to her prayers, scorning the many Phaeacian suitors. Through someone else's insolence she can say what modesty forbids her to say directly. She then states her own principle, that she would blame a girl who consorted with men 'before the day of open marriage'.

sources.cite: I. J. F. de Jong, 'The Voice of Anonymity: tis-Speeches in the Iliad', Eranos 85 (1987) 69-84
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 6.273-88

title: Supplicate the queen
greek: μητρὸς ἀμφὶ γούνασι χεῖρας βάλλειν (mētros amphi gounasi cheiras ballein)
short: Nausicaa tells Odysseus to pass by the king and clasp the queen's knees, for if Arete favours him he will reach home.
body: The instruction is surprising: the suppliant is to bypass the king, seated beside his wife at the same pillar (Merry discusses the arrangement of the two seats), and address the queen. Athena repeats almost the same words (7.75-7), and the poem's description of Arete's authority (7.66-74) explains why. Scholars have debated the reason for this emphasis: some see a trace of a society in which royal women held special power, others the poem's general interest in queens such as Penelope and Helen, or simply the fact that the queen's goodwill decides how a guest is treated in a household. In the event Arete does not reply to Odysseus immediately; it is the old Echeneus and Alcinous who act (7.155-71), and her decisive question comes later (7.237-9).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 6.308-10

title: Athena's fear of Poseidon
greek: αἴδετο γάρ ῥα πατροκασίγνητον (aideto gar rha patrokasignēton)
short: Athena hears Odysseus' prayer but does not appear openly, out of respect for her uncle Poseidon, who rages on until Odysseus reaches home.
body: Odysseus' reproach that Athena 'did not hearken' when Poseidon wrecked him (6.325-6) raises a question the poem answers only obliquely: why was the goddess absent during the Wanderings? Here Homer gives one reason, her 'respect' (aideto) for Poseidon, her father's brother. Merry explains that the gods avoid openly opposing one another. Athena later gives Odysseus the same explanation herself (13.341-3). The pattern is consistent: she acts only after Poseidon has gone (5.382-7) and appears in disguise in Scheria (7.19-20, 8.193-4). Poseidon's anger is the motive force of Odysseus' sufferings from the blinding of Polyphemus (1.68-75) until the punishment of the Phaeacians.
